blocks.html: In First Writing you met naming words (nouns), action words (verbs) and describing words. Grammar gives every word in a sentence a name for the job it does. These jobs are called the parts of speech.

head: Part of speech
Its job
Examples
rows: names a person, place, thing or idea
shows an action or a state of being
tells how, when, where or how much
links a noun to another word
joins words or groups of words
shows feeling, apart from the rest
blocks.cap: The eight traditional parts of speech.

blocks.name: wr-tag

opts.text: Wow|int, the|adj tiny|adj kitten|n quickly|adv climbed|v up|prep the|adj tree|n and|conj she|pro meowed|v!

blocks.cap: One sentence with all eight parts of speech. Each color is a job.

blocks.html: A word’s part of speech is the job it does in its sentence. To name it, ask what the word is doing here.
Naming the jobs lets us talk about sentences: why one is unclear, where a comma goes, why a verb must change. Every later topic in this course, from subjects to diagrams, uses these eight names.

blocks.title: Name the jobs
blocks.q: What part of speech is each word in “Leo carefully painted the old fence”?
steps: Leo names a person: noun.
painted shows the action: verb.
carefully tells how he painted: adverb.
old describes the fence: adjective. The is an adjective too (an article).
fence names a thing: noun.
blocks.a: noun, adverb, verb, adjective, adjective, noun

blocks.title: The same word, two jobs
blocks.q: What part of speech is run in “We run every morning” and in “Dad went for a long run”?
steps: In the first sentence, run is what we do: a verb.
In the second, a long comes before it and it names a thing Dad went for: a noun.

blocks.html: Memorizing lists (“run is a verb”) and labeling words without looking at the sentence. Many words can do more than one job. Check the job: does the word name, act, describe, tell how, link, join, stand in for a noun, or show feeling?

blocks.name: wr-tag

opts.text: Oh|int, we|pro forgot|v the|adj tickets|n again|adv.

blocks.cap: Your turn: choose a label, tap the words that do that job, then Check.

blocks.html: Grammar books don’t all count the same way. The eight above are the traditional list, used by older books such as Reed and Kellogg’s Higher Lessons in English and by many schools. Some modern books add articles or determiners (a, the, this, my) as a ninth group. This course calls a, an and the adjectives, as the traditional list does. For more practice in the old style, see the site’s Mother Tongue and Harvey’s grammar pages.

blocks.html: A noun names a person, a place, a thing or an idea (The Eight Parts of Speech). Nouns come in several kinds, and one noun can belong to more than one kind at once.

head: Kind
What it names
Examples
rows: one particular one; starts with a capital
something you can see, hear, touch, taste or smell
a feeling, a quality or an idea

blocks.html: Every noun names something, even when you can’t touch it. Courage and idea are nouns just as much as rock and apple.

Knowing the kinds helps with writing. Proper nouns need capital letters. Collective nouns raise questions about which verb to use (“The team is ready”). And abstract nouns let us write about the things that matter most: kindness, freedom, hope.

blocks.title: Find the nouns
blocks.q: Which words are nouns in “The team showed great courage in the final game”?
steps: team names a group: a collective noun.
courage names a quality: an abstract noun.
game names a thing: a concrete, common noun.
Test each one: you can put the in front of it.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: A quality. You can see kind acts, but not kindness itself.
You can hear it, so it is concrete.
A time of life: an idea, not a thing to touch.

blocks.cap: Sort the nouns. Ask: could you see, hear, touch, taste or smell it?

blocks.html: Skipping abstract nouns because you can’t see or touch them. Test any word: can it follow the or his or her (“her honesty,” “the idea”)? Can it be the subject of a verb (“Honesty matters”)? Then it is a noun.

blocks.html: A pronoun stands in for a noun, so we don’t repeat it (Kinds of Nouns). Instead of “Mia said Mia lost Mia’s hat,” we write “Mia said she lost her hat.”
Personal pronouns change their form for person (who is speaking or spoken about), number (one or more) and case (the job in the sentence).

head: Subject
Object
Possessive (before a noun)
Possessive (alone)
blocks.cap: First person speaks, second person is spoken to, third person is spoken about.

blocks.html: Use the subject form for a subject (She laughed), the object form after a verb or preposition (Grandma hugged her; a note for her), and a possessive form to show ownership (her hat; the hat is hers).
Pronouns keep writing smooth, but only if the reader can tell what each one stands for and what job it does. The forms carry that information: he is doing something; him is receiving it.

blocks.title: Replace the nouns
blocks.q: “Ana and Leo thanked Grandpa for Grandpa’s help.” Replace the repeated nouns with pronouns.
steps: Ana and Leo is the subject, more than one, spoken about: They.
Grandpa’s shows ownership before a noun: his.

blocks.name: wr-tag

opts.text: She|pro gave|v me|pro her|pro old|adj bike|n, and|conj now|adv it|pro is|v mine|pro.

blocks.cap: Tap every pronoun, then Check.

blocks.html: Getting stuck when two books disagree about my, your and her before a noun. Some grammars call them possessive pronouns, some call them possessive adjectives, and some call them determiners. All agree on what matters: they show ownership and come before a noun. Mine, yours and hers stand alone.

blocks.html: Besides personal pronouns, English has several other kinds. Each does a different job.

head: Kind
Job
Examples
rows: points back to the subject; the sentence needs it
adds emphasis; the sentence works without it
points to something: this, that, these, those
starts a clause that describes a noun

blocks.html: To tell reflexive from intensive, take the -self word out. If the sentence breaks, it is reflexive. If it still works, it is intensive.

Each kind solves a problem. Reflexives let the subject act on itself. Intensives add stress (“the mayor herself”). Indefinites let us talk about people we can’t or don’t need to name. Relatives connect a describing clause to its noun.

blocks.title: Reflexive or intensive?
blocks.q: “We painted the whole room ourselves.”
steps: Take ourselves out: “We painted the whole room.”
The sentence still works and means the same thing.
So ourselves only adds emphasis.

blocks.title: Pronoun or not?
blocks.q: Is this a pronoun in “This song is my favorite”?
steps: A noun, song, comes right after this.
This tells which song, so here it works like an adjective (some books say a determiner).
In “This is my favorite,” nothing follows it, so there it is a demonstrative pronoun.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: Leo hurt himself on the stairs.
The chef himself served the soup.
The cat saw itself in the mirror.

cards.why: Take it out: “We built the fort.” Still complete.

blocks.cap: Take out the -self word. Does the sentence break?

blocks.html: Calling this, that, these and those pronouns even when a noun follows them. In “those pears,” those describes the noun. It is a pronoun only when it stands alone: “Those are ripe.”

blocks.html: Every sentence has a verb (The Eight Parts of Speech). Most verbs show an action: run, paint, think. Some verbs show no action at all. A linking verb joins the subject to a word that renames it or describes it.

items: Forms of be: am, is, are, was, were, be, been, being.
Verbs like be: seem, become, appear, remain.
Sense verbs: look, feel, smell, taste, sound; also grow and turn (“grew dark,” “turned orange”).

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The soup smelled delicious.

blocks.cap: Smelled links the soup to a word that describes it.

blocks.html: The test: swap in is or was. If the sentence still makes sense with the same meaning, the verb is linking. If it turns into nonsense, the verb shows action.

The difference changes what follows the verb. After an action verb, a noun can receive the action (a direct object). After a linking verb, the word that follows tells about the subject. Diagrams, pronoun choices and adjective-or-adverb questions all depend on it.

blocks.title: Same verb, two jobs
blocks.q: Is felt action or linking in “Ana felt the fabric” and in “The fabric felt soft”?
steps: Swap in was: “Ana was the fabric.” Nonsense, so in the first sentence felt is an action: Ana touched it.
Swap in was: “The fabric was soft.” That works, so in the second sentence felt is linking.

blocks.html: Thinking every verb is an action and missing is and seems; or the opposite, calling look and feel linking even when they show action (“She looked at the stars”). Don’t judge by the word. Use the swap test on the sentence.

blocks.cap: Use the swap test on each card.

blocks.html: A verb can be more than one word. In “Leo has been practicing,” the main verb practicing has two helping verbs (also called auxiliary verbs) in front of it. Together they make a verb phrase. This builds on Action and Linking Verbs.

head: Helping verbs
Examples
rows: forms of be: am, is, are, was, were, be, been, being
forms of have: have, has, had
forms of do: do, does, did
modals: can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would

blocks.html: The verb phrase is the main verb plus every helping verb in front of it. Not and never are not part of it: they are adverbs.

Helping verbs carry time and meaning: will points to the future, has links the past to now, might shows a possibility, must shows need. The whole phrase is one verb, so it stays together on the baseline when you diagram it.

blocks.title: A phrase with not
blocks.q: What is the verb phrase in “Mia has not finished her book”?
steps: The main verb is finished.
The helping verb in front of it is has.
Not tells about the verb (it is an adverb), so leave it out.

blocks.title: A split verb in a question
blocks.q: What is the verb phrase in “Did the bus leave early?”
steps: Turn it into a statement: “The bus did leave early.”
The helping verb did and the main verb leave belong together.

blocks.cap: Tap every word of both verb phrases (not the word not), then Check.

blocks.html: Marking only the last word as the verb (only running in “has been running”), or counting not and n’t as part of the verb. Take every helping verb, and leave out the adverbs that sit inside the phrase.

blocks.html: An adjective modifies (describes or limits) a noun or pronoun (Kinds of Nouns). It answers one of three questions: which one? (that bike), what kind? (a red bike), how many? (three bikes).
Three small words are adjectives too: the articles a, an and the. Use an before a vowel sound (an apple, an hour) and a before a consonant sound (a kite, a unicorn).

blocks.name: wr-tag

opts.text: The|adj three|adj hungry|adj ducks|n ate|- the|adj old|adj bread|n.

blocks.cap: Every adjective here comes right before the noun it describes.

blocks.html: An adjective can come before its noun (the hot soup) or after a linking verb (the soup is hot). Either way, it describes the noun.

Adjectives let a reader see what you see. “A dog” could be any dog; “a small, muddy dog” is one the reader can picture. Knowing where they can sit also helps later, when you choose between an adjective and an adverb (“The soup smells good,” not “well”).

blocks.title: Find every adjective
blocks.q: “The old blanket felt soft.”
steps: The is an article: an adjective.
old tells what kind of blanket.
soft comes after the linking verb felt, but it describes the blanket.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The lemonade tasted sour.

blocks.cap: A predicate adjective sits after the verb but points back to the subject.

blocks.html: Missing adjectives that come after a linking verb (“The soup is hot”), and forgetting that a, an and the count. Look before each noun and after each linking verb.

blocks.html: An adverb modifies a verb, an adjective or another adverb. It answers how? (slowly), when? (soon), where? (outside), how often? (often) or how much? (very). It builds on Adjectives and Articles and Action and Linking Verbs.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The very old horse ran quite slowly.

blocks.cap: Three adverbs: very modifies an adjective, quite modifies an adverb, slowly modifies the verb.

blocks.html: Find an adverb by its job, not its ending. Ask which word it tells about, and what it tells: how, when, where, how often or how much.

Adverbs make actions precise: “ran” versus “ran slowly” or “nearly ran.” Words like not, never, very and too are some of the most common adverbs in English, and they can change a sentence’s whole meaning.

blocks.title: Not every adverb ends in -ly
blocks.q: Find the adverb: “The friendly neighbor waved often.”
steps: friendly ends in -ly, but it describes the neighbor, a noun. It is an adjective.
often tells how often the neighbor waved. It is the adverb.

blocks.title: What does it modify?
blocks.q: In “The soup was too hot,” what does too modify?
steps: too tells how hot.
hot is an adjective.

blocks.html: Thinking every adverb ends in -ly. Then you miss very, often, soon, fast, not and here, and you call friendly, lovely and lonely adverbs when they are adjectives. Check the job.

blocks.name: wr-sort
blocks.cap: Sort by the job in the example, not by the ending.

blocks.html: A preposition shows how a noun or pronoun relates to another word in the sentence. The noun or pronoun after it is its object. Together they make a prepositional phrase: in the box, after lunch, with Sam. This builds on Kinds of Nouns.

Common prepositions: about, above, across, after, against, along, around, at, before, behind, below, beside, between, by, down, during, for, from, in, into, near, of, off, on, over, past, through, to, toward, under, until, up, with, without.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The cat slept under the warm blanket.

blocks.cap: Under relates its object, blanket, to where the cat slept.

blocks.html: A preposition always has an object. Ask “preposition what?” or “preposition whom?”: under what? the blanket.

Prepositions carry the relations between things: place (under, beside), time (after, during), direction (to, toward) and more. Finding the object also keeps you from a common trap: the subject of a sentence is never inside a prepositional phrase.

blocks.title: Preposition or adverb?
blocks.q: Is up a preposition in “She climbed up the ladder” and in “She looked up”?
steps: “Up what?” In the first, the ladder: it has an object, so up is a preposition.
In the second, nothing follows: up tells where she looked. It is an adverb.

blocks.html: Calling words like up, down, in, out and around prepositions every time. With no object after them (“Please sit down”), they are adverbs.

opts.text: After|prep lunch|- we|- walked|- along|prep the|- river|- and|- sat|- down|- near|prep the|- old|- bridge|-.

blocks.cap: Tap each preposition. Careful: one of these words has no object.

blocks.html: A conjunction joins words, phrases or clauses. There are three kinds. This builds on Prepositions and Adverbs.

head: Kind
What it does
Examples
rows: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so (FANBOYS)
starts a dependent clause and ties it to the rest
after, although, as, because, before, if, since, though, unless, until, when, while
both … and, either … or, neither … nor, not only … but also, whether … or

blocks.html: Coordinating conjunctions join equals. Subordinating conjunctions make the clause they start lean on another clause: “because it rained” can’t stand alone.
Conjunctions show how ideas relate: and adds, but contrasts, so gives a result, because gives a reason, although admits something. Choosing the right one makes your thinking clear to the reader.

blocks.title: Preposition or conjunction?
blocks.q: What is after in “We left after the game” and in “We left after the game ended”?
steps: In the first, only a noun follows (the game): after is a preposition.
In the second, a clause follows, with its own subject and verb (the game ended): after is a subordinating conjunction.

blocks.name: wr-sort
blocks.cap: Sort the conjunctions by kind.

blocks.html: Treating because and although like and and but. They are not the same: a clause that starts with because is dependent and can’t be a sentence by itself (“Because it rained.” is a fragment). Also watch after, before, since and until: look at what follows them.

blocks.html: An interjection is a word or short phrase that shows feeling: wow, oh, oops, hooray, ouch, well, hmm. It isn’t tied into the grammar of the sentence; it stands apart. It is the last of the eight parts of speech (Conjunctions came just before).

items: A strong interjection can stand alone with an exclamation point. The next sentence starts with a capital: “Ouch! That pan is hot.”
An interjection can also be set off with a comma inside the sentence: “Ouch, that pan is hot!”
A mild interjection takes a comma: “Well, maybe tomorrow.” “Oh, I see.”

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: well maybe we can go tomorrow
answer: Well, maybe we can go tomorrow.

blocks.cap: Add the marks and the capital. Tap a gap for a mark; tap a word to switch its capital.

blocks.html: An interjection shows feeling and is set off from the sentence: with a comma when it is mild or part of the sentence, with an exclamation point when it stands alone.
In speech, your voice shows feeling. On paper, interjections and their punctuation do that job. The marks also tell the reader that the word isn’t the subject or any other part of the sentence.

blocks.title: Two correct ways
blocks.q: Punctuate: “hooray we won”
steps: Hooray shows strong feeling.
It can stand alone: “Hooray! We won!”
Or it can join the sentence with a comma: “Hooray, we won!”
blocks.a: Either “Hooray! We won!” or “Hooray, we won!”

blocks.html: Thinking every interjection needs an exclamation point. “Oh! I see.” makes a quiet thought sound like a shout. A mild interjection takes a comma: “Oh, I see.”

blocks.html: You have now met all eight parts of speech, from nouns to interjections. Here is the big idea that ties them together: a word doesn’t have one part of speech forever. It has the part of speech of the job it does in this sentence.

head: Sentence
light is a …
Because
rows: it names a thing; the comes before it
it is the action, and we is its subject
it tells what kind of jacket

blocks.html: Decide a word’s part of speech by its job here: what comes before and after it, and what it does for the sentence.
English reuses words all the time: you can water the plants, drink water, and buy a water bottle. Dictionaries list every job a word can do; only the sentence tells you which one it is doing now.

blocks.title: Clues around the word
blocks.q: What is back in “Sign your name on the back of the card,” “Please come back soon,” and “We used the back door”?
steps: the back of the card: the before it, and it names a part: noun.
come back: it tells where to come: adverb.
the back door: it tells which door: adjective.

blocks.title: A trickier one
blocks.q: What is but in “Everyone but Sam came to the picnic”?
steps: Here but means “except.”
It has an object, Sam, and links it to everyone.
So here it is a preposition, not a conjunction.

blocks.html: Looking a word up and taking the first part of speech the dictionary lists. The dictionary lists them all. Read the sentence and check the job.

blocks.html: In What Is a Sentence? you learned that a sentence tells who or what and what happens. Grammar names those two halves. The complete subject is who or what the sentence is about. The complete predicate is everything said about it.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The girl with the red kite ran across the field.

blocks.cap: Every word belongs to one half or the other.

blocks.html: Find the predicate by finding the verb. Everything from the verb on (and its helping verbs) is usually the complete predicate; the words before it that name who or what make the complete subject.
A sentence makes a claim about something. The subject says what the claim is about; the predicate makes the claim. If either half is missing, the reader is left with a fragment.

blocks.title: A long subject
blocks.q: Split: “The box of old crayons fell off the shelf.”
steps: The verb is fell.
What fell? The box of old crayons: the whole group of words before the verb.
What is said about it? fell off the shelf.
blocks.a: The box of old crayons | fell off the shelf.

blocks.title: A subject that is a thing
blocks.q: Split: “The old bridge creaked in the wind.”
steps: The verb is creaked.
What creaked? The old bridge. Subjects can be things, places and ideas, not just people.
blocks.a: The old bridge | creaked in the wind.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: My little brother with the red hat laughed at the clown.

blocks.cap: Tap the first word of the complete predicate, then Check.

blocks.html: Thinking the subject is always the first word, or always a person. In “After lunch, the class went outside,” the sentence starts with After lunch, but the subject is the class. Ask the question: who or what does the verb tell about?

blocks.html: Inside the complete subject is one key word, the simple subject: the noun or pronoun the sentence is about. Inside the complete predicate is the simple predicate: the verb, with any helping verbs.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: One of the dogs has been barking all night.

blocks.cap: Cross out the prepositional phrase. The simple subject is One, and the verb is has been barking.

blocks.html: To find the simple subject, cross out prepositional phrases first. The subject is never inside one.

The verb must agree with the simple subject: “One of the dogs has,” not “have.” If you take dogs for the subject, you choose the wrong verb. The simple subject and the verb are also the skeleton you draw first in a sentence diagram.

blocks.title: Cross out, then find
blocks.q: Find the simple subject and the verb: “The basket of ripe apples sits by the door.”
steps: Cross out of ripe apples and by the door.
Left: “The basket sits.”
The simple subject is basket; the verb is sits.

blocks.title: A verb phrase
blocks.q: Find the simple predicate: “The tired hikers will be resting soon.”
steps: The main verb is resting.
The helping verbs will be belong with it.
Soon is an adverb, not part of the verb.

blocks.html: Choosing a noun inside a prepositional phrase as the subject: in “One of the dogs barks,” the subject is One, not dogs. This one slip causes many agreement errors later (“One of the dogs bark”). Cross out the phrase first.

blocks.html: In most sentences the subject comes before the verb (Simple Subject and Verb). Four kinds of sentences hide it.

head: Kind
Example
Turn it around
Subject
rows: There are three apples in the bowl.
Three apples are in the bowl.
Under the bridge lived a troll.
A troll lived under the bridge.

blocks.html: Put the sentence back in the usual order: subject, then verb. There and here are almost never the subject, and a command’s subject is you, understood.
English moves words around to ask, to point and to command. The subject is still there, and the verb still has to agree with it: “There are three apples” because apples is plural.

blocks.title: A command with a name
blocks.q: What is the subject of “Leo, feed the cat”?
steps: The sentence tells someone to do something: it is a command.
A command’s subject is you, understood.
Leo is the person spoken to, set off by a comma: a noun of direct address, not the subject.

blocks.title: There
blocks.q: What is the subject of “There goes the bus”?
steps: Turn it around: “The bus goes there.”
What goes? The bus.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: The parade comes here: the subject is parade.
Mia is spoken to; the subject is (you).

cards.text: There were two owls on the fence.

blocks.cap: Does the sentence state its subject, or is it you, understood?

blocks.html: Calling there or here the subject, and saying a command like “Sit down” has no subject. Turn the sentence around; for a command, put you in front.

blocks.html: In First Writing you learned the end marks for telling, asking and exclaiming. Grammar names four kinds of sentences by what they do. Commands are one of them; their subject is often you, understood (Hard-to-Find Subjects).

head: Kind
What it does
Usual end mark
Example
rows: gives a command or makes a request
What a huge library this is!

blocks.html: Name the kind by the sentence’s purpose, then choose the end mark that fits. The end mark follows the purpose, not the other way around.
Writers mix the four kinds to talk to readers: a question pulls them in, a command tells them what to do, an exclamation shows feeling. Knowing the purpose also settles the end mark.

blocks.title: A question word inside a statement
blocks.q: What kind of sentence is “I wonder who won the game”?
steps: It has the question word who.
But it only reports a question; no one has to answer it.
It makes a statement, so it is declarative and ends with a period.

blocks.title: A command with an exclamation point
blocks.q: What kind of sentence is “Close the door!”?
steps: It tells someone to do something.
The exclamation point adds force, but the purpose is still to command.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: Leo asked where the fish food was.
cards.why: It reports a question; it doesn’t ask one.

cards.text: What a hungry fish that is!

cards.why: A warning is a command, even with an exclamation point.

blocks.cap: Sort by what each sentence does.

blocks.html: Judging by the end mark alone. “Close the door!” ends with an exclamation point but gives a command. (Some books call a forceful command an exclamatory command; its purpose is still to command.) Ask what the sentence does.

blocks.html: A sentence can have two or more simple subjects that share one verb, or two or more verbs that share one subject. The parts are joined by a conjunction, usually and or or.

items: Compound subject: Ana and Leo sang.
Compound verb: Leo sang and danced.
Both: Ana and Leo sang and danced.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: Ana and Leo sang and danced.

blocks.cap: A sentence diagram shows the two subjects and the two verbs as forks on one baseline. (Diagrams come in the last unit.)

blocks.html: A compound subject or a compound verb still makes one clause and one sentence. Don’t put a comma before the and of a compound verb.

Compound parts let you say two things at once without repeating: “Leo sang. Leo danced.” becomes “Leo sang and danced.” A comma before and signals a second sentence is coming, so it would mislead the reader here.

blocks.title: The comma question
blocks.q: Which is right: “Mia washed the dishes, and dried them” or “Mia washed the dishes and dried them”?
steps: After and comes dried them: no new subject.
So washed … and dried is a compound verb in one clause.
No comma is needed.
blocks.a: “Mia washed the dishes and dried them.”

blocks.html: Mistaking a compound verb for two sentences and adding a comma: “She ran, and jumped.” Check what follows and. If it has its own subject (“and she jumped”), the comma belongs; if not, leave it out.

blocks.html: Many action verbs pass their action on to something. That word is the direct object. It answers whom? or what? after the verb. It builds on Simple Subject and Verb.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: Mia kicked the ball over the fence.

blocks.cap: Kicked what? The ball. Fence is the object of the preposition over, not of the verb.

blocks.html: Find the verb, then ask “verb what?” or “verb whom?” The answer, if it is a noun or pronoun outside a prepositional phrase, is the direct object.

The direct object completes the meaning of many verbs. “Leo fixed” leaves you asking what; “Leo fixed the bike” is whole. The object also takes the object form of a pronoun: “Leo fixed it,” “saw her,” never “saw she.”

blocks.title: Which noun?
blocks.q: Find the direct object: “Grandpa planted tulips in the garden.”
steps: The verb is planted.
Planted what? tulips.
Garden sits inside the phrase in the garden, so it is the object of the preposition.

blocks.title: No direct object
blocks.q: Does “Mia became the captain” have a direct object?
steps: Became is a linking verb: no action passes on.
Captain renames Mia. It is a predicate noun (a later topic), not a direct object.

blocks.html: Calling any noun after the verb a direct object. Two kinds of nouns are not: a noun after a linking verb (it renames the subject) and the object of a preposition. Check that the verb shows action and that the noun isn’t inside a phrase.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: Door is the object of the preposition by.
Is is a linking verb; pilot renames Ana.

cards.text: The baby slept in the car.

blocks.cap: Ask “verb what?” for each card.

blocks.html: Some verbs, like give, send, show, tell, make and buy, can take two objects. The direct object is what is given or made. The indirect object tells to whom or for whom.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: Grandma gave Sam a book.

blocks.cap: Gave what? a book (direct object). To whom? Sam (indirect object).

blocks.html: The indirect object comes between the verb and the direct object, with no to or for in front of it. A sentence can have an indirect object only if it also has a direct object.

English has two ways to say the same thing: “gave Sam a book” and “gave a book to Sam.” Grammar labels them differently because the words do different jobs. In the second, Sam is the object of the preposition to.

blocks.title: Two objects
blocks.q: Find both objects: “The coach handed the team a map.”
steps: Handed what? a map: the direct object.
To whom? the team: the indirect object, between the verb and the direct object.

blocks.title: The to version
blocks.q: Does “She gave the map to Sam” have an indirect object?
steps: The direct object is map.
to Sam is a prepositional phrase. Sam is the object of the preposition.

blocks.html: Swapping the two objects. The indirect object comes first and is the person (or thing) receiving: in “Dad baked us a pie,” us is indirect and pie is direct. Check: can you move it after to or for (“baked a pie for us”)? Then it is the indirect object.

blocks.html: After a linking verb, the word that completes the sentence points back to the subject. Grammar calls it a subject complement, and it comes in two kinds.

items: A predicate noun renames the subject: “Ana became captain.” (Ana = the captain.)
A predicate adjective describes the subject: “Ana is tall.” (a tall Ana)

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: My sister became the captain, and she seemed proud.

blocks.cap: Both complements point back to their subjects.

blocks.html: After a linking verb, nothing receives an action. A noun there renames the subject (predicate noun); an adjective there describes it (predicate adjective).

This explains choices that sound odd at first. After a sense verb, standard usage takes an adjective, not an adverb: “The soup smells good” describes the soup. And formal writing has traditionally used the subject form of a pronoun after be (“It was she who called”), though “It was her” is common and widely accepted in speech; usage guides differ on how formal to be.

blocks.title: Direct object or predicate noun?
blocks.q: “Leo painted the fence” and “Leo became the painter.”
steps: Painted is an action; the fence receives it: direct object.
Became is linking; the painter is Leo: predicate noun.

blocks.name: wr-sort
blocks.cap: What job does the bold word do?

blocks.html: Calling a predicate noun a direct object. In “Ana became captain,” captain is Ana, so it renames her; nothing receives an action. Check the verb first: linking or action?

blocks.html: A few verbs, like name, call, elect, make, keep, find and paint, can take a word after the direct object that renames or describes it. That word is an object complement. It works like a subject complement, but for the object.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: They named the puppy Biscuit.

blocks.cap: Named whom? the puppy. Named it what? Biscuit: the puppy is Biscuit.

blocks.html: An object complement follows the direct object and is the same person or thing (a noun) or describes it (an adjective): “The news made Dad happy.”

The object complement finishes what the verb does to the object. “They painted the door” is complete, but “They painted the door red” tells the result. “The class elected Mia” is complete, but “elected Mia president” says to what.

blocks.title: Object complement or indirect object?
blocks.q: Compare “They named the puppy Biscuit” with “They gave the puppy a bone.”
steps: In the first, Biscuit and the puppy are the same: Biscuit is an object complement, and puppy is the direct object.
In the second, a bone and the puppy are different things: bone is the direct object, and puppy is the indirect object (gave to whom?).

blocks.html: Reading “named the puppy Biscuit” as an indirect object and a direct object. Test with “is”: the puppy is Biscuit, so the two words are the same thing, and the second completes the first. With an indirect object, the test fails: the puppy is not a bone.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: The team gave Leo a medal.
cards.why: Leo is not a medal: indirect object and direct object.

cards.text: The rain made the path muddy.
The blanket kept the baby warm.
Grandpa told the kids a story.

blocks.cap: Use the “is” test on the last two nouns or words.

blocks.html: Older grammars use different names. Reed and Kellogg’s Higher Lessons in English calls the direct object the “object complement” and this lesson’s object complement the “objective complement.” Most textbooks today use the names in this lesson.

blocks.html: A prepositional phrase is a preposition, its object, and any words that describe the object: with the red kite, after lunch. The whole phrase works like one modifier, and it can do one of two jobs.

items: An adjective phrase modifies a noun or pronoun. It tells which one or what kind: “the girl with the kite.”
An adverb phrase modifies a verb, adjective or adverb. It tells where, when, how or why: “ran to the park,” “left after lunch.”

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The girl with the kite ran to the park.

blocks.cap: One phrase tells which girl; the other tells where she ran.

blocks.html: Ask which word the phrase tells more about. A noun: it is an adjective phrase. A verb (or an adjective or adverb): it is an adverb phrase.

Putting a phrase next to the right word keeps meaning clear. “I saw a deer with binoculars” could mean the deer had binoculars. Knowing what a phrase modifies is the first step to fixing a misplaced modifier, and it decides where the phrase hangs in a diagram.

blocks.title: Which word does it modify?
blocks.q: “Leo kicked the ball over the fence.” What does over the fence modify?
steps: The nearest noun is ball, but the phrase doesn’t tell which ball.
It tells where Leo kicked: it modifies the verb kicked.

blocks.title: Two phrases in a row
blocks.q: “The box of crayons on the shelf is mine.”
steps: of crayons tells which box: adjective phrase.
on the shelf also tells which box: another adjective phrase.

blocks.html: Deciding by position, as if a phrase always modifies the word right before it. Ask the questions: which one? (adjective phrase) or where, when, how, why? (adverb phrase).

blocks.html: An appositive is a noun or noun phrase placed right beside another noun to rename it: “My aunt, a pilot, flew us home.” It works like a predicate noun that needs no verb, and like a modifier it sits next to the word it tells about.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: Jupiter, the largest planet, has many moons.

blocks.cap: The appositive renames Jupiter. Take it out and the sentence still works.

blocks.html: Commas depend on whether the appositive is needed to tell which one. If it only adds information, set it off with commas. If it identifies which one, use no commas.

Commas tell the reader “this is extra.” “My brother, Leo, plays chess” says you have one brother and adds his name. “My brother Leo plays chess” uses the name to pick out which brother, so it suggests you have more than one.

blocks.title: Commas or not?
blocks.q: Ana has two brothers. Punctuate: “Ana’s brother Leo plays chess.”
steps: She has two brothers, so Leo tells which one.
An appositive that tells which one is needed: no commas.

blocks.title: A longer appositive
blocks.q: Find the appositive: “We read Charlotte’s Web, a book about a pig and a spider.”
steps: a book about a pig and a spider renames Charlotte’s Web.
It adds information (there is only one Charlotte’s Web), so a comma sets it off.
blocks.a: a book about a pig and a spider

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: Mr. Lee our coach blew the whistle
answer: Mr. Lee, our coach, blew the whistle.

blocks.cap: There is only one coach. Add the commas and the period.

blocks.html: Leaving out the commas around an appositive that only adds information, or adding commas around one that tells which person or thing is meant (“my friend, Ana,” when you have many friends). Ask: without it, would the reader know which one?

blocks.html: Words work in groups. You have met prepositional phrases, appositives and compound subjects and verbs. Every group of words is either a phrase or a clause.

items: A clause has its own subject and its own verb: the bell rang, because she was tired.
A phrase lacks a subject, a verb, or both: after the long game, was waiting, to win the race.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: Running is a verbal, and there is no subject.

cards.text: the girl in the red coat
cards.why: A noun and its modifiers, but no verb.

blocks.cap: Look for a subject and a verb that go together.

blocks.html: A clause = a subject + its verb. No pair, no clause, however long the group is.
Clauses are the building blocks of sentences. Every sentence has at least one; how many it has, and how they are joined, decides its structure and its punctuation.

blocks.title: Same start, different groups
blocks.q: Phrase or clause: “before breakfast” and “before we ate breakfast”?
steps: “before breakfast” has no verb: a phrase.
“before we ate breakfast” has the subject we and the verb ate: a clause.

blocks.html: Thinking any long group of words is a clause, or that a clause has to be a whole sentence. “The tall girl in the bright red coat by the door” is long but has no verb: a phrase. “Because it rained” is short, has a subject and a verb, and is a clause, though not a sentence.

blocks.html: Every clause has a subject and a verb. Some clauses can stand alone as sentences; some can’t. The difference is often one small word at the front, a subordinating conjunction or a relative pronoun.

head: Independent clause
Dependent clause
blocks.cap: Add one word, and the clause leans on another one.

blocks.html: An independent clause can stand alone as a sentence. A dependent clause (also called a subordinate clause) begins with a word like because, when, if, who or that, and it can’t stand alone.

A dependent clause leaves the reader waiting: “When the bell rang …” what happened? It must be attached to an independent clause that finishes the thought: “When the bell rang, we went home.” Written alone, it is a fragment.

blocks.title: Find the dependent clause
blocks.q: “We waited patiently although the bus was late.”
steps: Two clauses: we waited patiently and although the bus was late.
The second starts with although and can’t stand alone.
The first could be a sentence by itself.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: When the bell rang, the students left.

blocks.cap: The dependent clause comes first here, so a comma follows it.

blocks.html: Writing a dependent clause as if it were a sentence: “Because it rained.” Read it alone. If it leaves you waiting for the rest, join it to an independent clause: “We stayed inside because it rained.”

blocks.html: Verbs can do other jobs. A verbal is a verb form used as another part of speech. The first kind is the participle: a verb form used as an adjective. Present participles end in -ing (barking); past participles usually end in -ed or -en (painted, broken). You met them inside verb phrases in Helping Verbs.

items: “the barking dog”: which dog? barking describes it.
“the broken vase”
A participial phrase is a participle with its own object or modifiers: “Waving her hat, Mia ran to the bus.”

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: Waving her hat, Mia ran to the bus.

blocks.cap: The participial phrase describes Mia.

blocks.html: A participle describes a noun. If an -ing or -ed word follows a helping verb (is, was, has), it is part of the verb phrase instead.

Participles pack an action into a description: “the dog that was barking” becomes “the barking dog.” A participial phrase at the start of a sentence must describe the subject right after the comma, or the sentence says something silly. That is the dangling modifier you will fix in Usage and Mechanics.

blocks.title: Participle or verb?
blocks.q: Compare “The dog is barking” and “The barking dog woke the baby.”
steps: In the first, barking follows the helping verb is: it is part of the verb phrase is barking.
In the second, barking tells which dog; the verb is woke. Here it is a participle.

blocks.html: Calling every -ing word a verb. In “the barking dog,” barking describes the dog, so it works as an adjective. Find the real verb of the sentence first; the other verb forms are verbals.

blocks.html: A gerund is an -ing verb form used as a noun. It names an activity: “Swimming is fun.” It looks exactly like a present participle; only the job is different.

head: Job
Example
blocks.cap: A gerund or gerund phrase can do any job a noun can do.

blocks.html: Same -ing form, three possible jobs: a gerund names an activity (noun); a participle describes a noun (adjective); after a helping verb, the word is part of the verb.

Gerunds let you talk about actions as things: you can like, start, finish, avoid or be good at an activity. A gerund phrase can be long (“Reading before bed every night helps me sleep”), but the whole phrase still does one noun job.

blocks.title: Three jobs for swimming
blocks.q: “Swimming keeps Grandpa strong.” “The swimming children splashed us.” “The children are swimming.”
steps: Swimming keeps …: it names the activity and is the subject: gerund.
The swimming children: it tells which children: participle.
are swimming: it follows a helping verb: part of the verb phrase.

blocks.name: wr-sort
blocks.cap: Sort by the job of the bold word.

blocks.html: Mixing up gerunds and participles. Ask: does the -ing word name an activity (could you put it or this activity in its place)? Then it is a gerund. Does it describe a noun? Then it is a participle.

blocks.html: The third verbal is the infinitive: to plus the base form of a verb (to win, to read, to help). After participles (adjectives) and gerunds (nouns), the infinitive is the busiest: it can do three jobs.

head: Job
Example
Test
rows: To win was her goal. Leo wants to learn the guitar.
It tells which or what kind of noun.
She came to help. The puppy was eager to play.
It tells why, or modifies an adjective.

blocks.html: An infinitive is to + a verb. To + a noun is a prepositional phrase, not an infinitive.

Infinitives let you name goals and purposes: what someone wants to do, why someone came, what something is for. The to + verb pattern is also why some readers object to a “split infinitive” (to boldly go). Most usage guides today accept splitting when it reads better; that debate comes up in Usage and Mechanics.

blocks.title: Infinitive or prepositional phrase?
blocks.q: “We walked to the park to play soccer.”
steps: to the park: to + a noun (park). A prepositional phrase.
to play soccer: to + the verb play. An infinitive phrase, telling why we walked: used as an adverb.

blocks.title: Name the job
blocks.q: “My plan is to finish early.”
steps: Replace it: “My plan is something.” That works.
So to finish early is used as a noun (a predicate noun after is).

blocks.html: Mixing up infinitives and prepositional phrases because both start with to. Look at the next word: a verb (to run) makes an infinitive; a noun or pronoun (to the store, to her) makes a prepositional phrase.

blocks.cap: Verb or noun after the to?

blocks.html: A dependent clause can do an adjective’s job. An adjective clause (also called a relative clause) follows a noun and tells which one or what kind. It usually begins with a relative pronoun: who, whom, whose, which or that (sometimes where or when).

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: The book that you lent me was funny.

blocks.cap: The clause tells which book. Inside it, that stands for the book.

blocks.html: An adjective clause comes right after the noun it modifies. Its relative pronoun does a job inside the clause (subject or object) and connects the clause to that noun.

Adjective clauses let you combine sentences: “I found a key. You lost it.” becomes “I found the key that you lost.” They also need careful commas: a clause that only adds information is set off with commas (“My uncle, who is a pilot, flew us home”); one that tells which one is not.

blocks.title: Find the clause and its noun
blocks.q: “The girl who won the race is my cousin.”
steps: The clause starts with who: who won the race.
Inside it, who is the subject and won the verb.
It tells which girl, so it modifies girl.

blocks.title: Not the nearest noun
blocks.q: “The boy with the kite that is stuck in the tree looks sad.” What is stuck?
steps: The clause that is stuck in the tree follows kite.
The kite is stuck, not the boy.

blocks.html: Ending the clause too early (taking only that you), or attaching it to the wrong noun. Take the whole clause, from the relative pronoun through its verb and everything that goes with it, and look at the noun just before it.

Which or that? American usage guides generally prefer that for a clause that tells which one (“the book that you lent me”) and which with commas for one that only adds information. Using which for the first kind is standard too, especially in British English. Usage and Mechanics goes into the details.

blocks.html: A dependent clause can also do an adverb’s job. An adverb clause begins with a subordinating conjunction and tells when, why, under what condition or in spite of what.

head: Tells
Conjunctions
Example
rows: when, after, before, while, until, as
If the rain stops, we will play.

blocks.html: An adverb clause can come before or after the main clause. When it comes first, a comma usually follows it. When it comes last, usually no comma.

Adverb clauses show how events connect: time, cause, condition, contrast. Moving the clause to the front puts that connection first (“Because the bridge was closed, we took the long way”), and the comma marks where the main clause begins.

blocks.title: Front or back
blocks.q: Punctuate both: “If you hurry you can catch the bus” and “You can catch the bus if you hurry.”
steps: In the first, the adverb clause If you hurry comes first: a comma follows it.
In the second, it comes last: no comma is needed.
blocks.a: “If you hurry, you can catch the bus.” / “You can catch the bus if you hurry.”

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: after the movie ended we walked home
answer: After the movie ended, we walked home.

blocks.cap: Add the capital, the comma after the adverb clause, and the period.

blocks.html: Thinking the dependent clause has to come second. It can come first; then a comma usually follows it. (With a short clause and no chance of misreading, some writers leave the comma out; the comma is never wrong there.)

blocks.html: The third kind of dependent clause does a noun’s job. A noun clause can be a subject, a direct object, an object of a preposition or a predicate noun, just like a gerund. It often begins with that, what, who, whoever, whether, if, how, why or where. Compare adjective clauses and adverb clauses.

head: Job
Example
rows: The prize goes to whoever finishes first.
My hope is that the rain stops.

blocks.html: The test: replace the clause with something or someone. If the sentence still works, it is a noun clause.

Noun clauses let you make a whole idea into a thing you can talk about: what someone said, whether it will rain, how a trick works. They are how we report thoughts and speech: “Leo asked if he could help.”

blocks.title: Noun clause or adjective clause?
blocks.q: Compare “We know who left the gate open” and “The boy who left the gate open said sorry.”
steps: First: “We know something.” Works. The clause is the direct object: a noun clause.
Second: “The boy something said sorry.” Doesn’t work. The clause tells which boy: an adjective clause.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: This is the spot where we parked.
I know that the store closes early.
The store that closes early is on Main Street.

blocks.cap: Use the “something” test on each bold clause.

blocks.html: Calling a noun clause an adjective clause because both can start with that, who or where. Don’t judge by the first word. An adjective clause follows a noun and describes it; a noun clause is itself the subject or an object.

blocks.html: Sentences are built from clauses (Independent and Dependent Clauses). Counting them tells you a sentence’s structure. The first two structures use only independent clauses.

items: A simple sentence has one independent clause. It can still be long, with phrases and compound parts: “Ana and her brother washed and dried the dishes after dinner.”

A compound sentence has two or more independent clauses, joined by a comma and a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) or by a semicolon: “The rain stopped, and the sun came out.” “The bell rang; class was over.”

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: Leo likes soccer, but Mia prefers chess.

blocks.cap: Two subject–verb pairs, each able to stand alone: a compound sentence.

blocks.html: Count subject–verb pairs that could each stand alone. One: simple. Two or more, joined: compound.

A compound sentence shows that two ideas are equal partners, and the conjunction says how they relate (and adds, but contrasts, so gives a result). The comma before the conjunction tells the reader a new clause is starting.

blocks.title: A compound verb is not a compound sentence
blocks.q: Is “Leo sang and danced at the party” simple or compound?
steps: Subject: Leo. Verbs: sang and danced.
After and there is no new subject, so there is only one clause.

blocks.title: Two clauses
blocks.q: Is “Leo sang, and Mia danced” simple or compound?
steps: First clause: Leo sang. Second clause: Mia danced.
Each could stand alone, and they are joined by a comma and and.

blocks.html: Calling a sentence with a compound verb a compound sentence. “Leo sang and danced” is simple: one subject, one clause. Check whether the words after the conjunction have their own subject.

blocks.html: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. The dependent clause can be an adverb clause, an adjective clause or a noun clause. Compare simple and compound sentences.

head: Structure
Independent clauses
Dependent clauses
Example
rows: The rain stopped, and the sun came out.
When the rain stopped, the sun came out.
When the rain stopped, the sun came out, and we went outside.
blocks.cap: The four structures, by their clauses.

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: When it rained, we left.

blocks.cap: Five words, and still complex: one dependent clause and one independent clause.

blocks.html: Complex means the sentence has a dependent clause, not that it is long or hard to read.

A complex sentence shows that one idea depends on another: the time, the reason, the condition. Mixing simple, compound and complex sentences makes writing flow and shows the reader how ideas connect.

blocks.title: A clause inside a clause
blocks.q: What structure is “The book that you lent me was funny”?
steps: The independent clause is The book was funny.
Inside it sits the adjective clause that you lent me, which can’t stand alone.
One independent clause and one dependent clause.

blocks.title: Long but simple
blocks.q: What structure is “After a long day at the beach, the tired children fell asleep in the car”?
steps: Find subject–verb pairs: only children fell.
After a long day, at the beach and in the car are phrases.

blocks.html: Thinking complex means long or hard. “When it rained, we left” is short and complex; the long beach sentence above is simple. Count the clauses, not the words.

blocks.html: The fourth structure combines the other two: a compound-complex sentence has two or more independent clauses (like a compound sentence) and at least one dependent clause (like a complex sentence).

blocks.name: wr-sentence

opts.text: When the bell rang, the students left, and the room was quiet.

blocks.cap: Two independent clauses and one dependent clause.

blocks.html: To name any structure: find every subject–verb pair, mark each as independent or dependent, then count.

Long, rich ideas often need this structure: two main events and the time or reason that ties them together. Knowing the parts also tells you where the commas go: after an opening dependent clause, and before the conjunction that joins the independent clauses.

blocks.title: A clause tucked inside
blocks.q: What structure is “The dog that lives next door barked, so we closed the window”?
steps: Independent clauses: The dog barked and we closed the window, joined by so.
Dependent clause: that lives next door, an adjective clause inside the first independent clause.
Two independent and one dependent.

blocks.title: Watch for verbals
blocks.q: What structure is “I wanted to go, but I stayed home because I was sick”?
steps: I wanted and I stayed home are independent clauses; to go is an infinitive, not a clause.
because I was sick is a dependent clause.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: The puppy barked; the kitten hid.
Mia smiled when she saw the puppy.
Running down the hill, Sam tripped.
cards.why: The participial phrase is not a clause.

cards.text: Since it was raining, we played inside, and Dad made popcorn.

cards.why: That she left is a noun clause.

cards.text: Mia and her brother washed and dried the dishes.

blocks.cap: Sort each sentence by its structure.

blocks.html: Miscounting when a dependent clause sits inside an independent one (“The dog that lives next door barked”), or counting a compound verb as two clauses. Mark every subject–verb pair before you count.

blocks.html: A sentence diagram is a picture of a sentence that puts every word where its job belongs. The kind used in American schools was published by Alonzo Reed and Brainerd Kellogg in Higher Lessons in English (1877). It starts with the two parts every sentence has: the simple subject and the verb.

items: Draw a horizontal baseline.
Write the simple subject on the left part.
Draw a short upright line that crosses the baseline. It splits the subject from the verb.
Write the verb, with all its helping verbs, on the right part.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: Leo has been waiting.

blocks.cap: The helping verbs stay with the main verb on the baseline.

blocks.html: Place each word by its job, not by its place in the sentence. Subject left, verb (with its helping verbs) right, on one baseline split by a line that crosses it.

A diagram shows what reading aloud can hide: which word is the subject, which is the verb, and how every other word hangs from them. In a question or a command the words are out of the usual order, but the diagram is the same, because the jobs are the same (Hard-to-Find Subjects).

blocks.title: A question
blocks.q: Diagram “Did Mia call?”
steps: Turn it around: “Mia did call.”
Subject: Mia. Verb: did call.
Write Mia left of the dividing line and did call right of it. (Some books keep the capital: Did call.)

blocks.title: A command
blocks.q: Diagram “Listen.”
steps: A command’s subject is you, understood.
Write it in parentheses: (you). The verb is Listen.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: Listen.

blocks.cap: The understood subject is written in parentheses.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: The twins were laughing.

blocks.cap: Your turn: tap a word, then tap its place (or drag it). Then Check. (The is already placed; it hangs under twins, as the next lesson explains.)

blocks.html: Copying the words in sentence order instead of placing each by its job, and putting helping verbs off the baseline. The whole verb phrase (were laughing, has been waiting) sits together right of the dividing line.

Textbooks draw a few details differently (the angle of a slant, where a conjunction sits). These lessons use the usual form, as in Reed and Kellogg’s Higher Lessons in English and most American grammars; if your book differs a little, both are fine.

Grokipedia, “Sentence diagram”

blocks.html: Once the subject and verb are on the baseline, modifiers hang below. Adjectives (articles too) and adverbs go on slanted lines under the word they modify.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: The small dog barked loudly.

blocks.cap: Press Next word to build the diagram one word at a time.

blocks.html: An adverb that modifies an adjective or another adverb hangs under that word, on a little shelf of its own.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: My very tall sister ran quite fast.

blocks.cap: Very hangs from tall, and quite hangs from fast.

blocks.html: Every modifier hangs on a slant under the exact word it tells about: adjectives under nouns, adverbs under verbs, adjectives or other adverbs.

The slanted lines make the modifier’s job visible. You can see at a glance that loudly describes the barking, not the dog. If a sentence is unclear, the diagram often shows why: a modifier could hang from two places.

blocks.title: Where does each word hang?
blocks.q: “The old owl hooted very softly.”
steps: Baseline: owl | hooted.
The and old describe the owl: slants under owl.
softly tells how it hooted: a slant under hooted.
very tells how softly: a slant under softly.
blocks.a: owl: The, old; hooted: softly; softly: very

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: The hungry puppy ate quickly.

blocks.cap: Build it: tap a word, then its place. Then Check.

blocks.html: Hanging an adverb that modifies an adjective under the noun. In “very tall sister,” very tells how tall, so it hangs from tall, not from sister.

sources.name: Alonzo Reed and Brainerd Kellogg, Higher Lessons in English (1877; revised edition 1896), Project Gutenberg eBook #7188 (public domain): the diagrams of Lessons 4–33
Grokipedia, “Sentence diagram”

blocks.html: A direct object goes on the baseline after the verb. An indirect object hangs under the verb. This builds on Diagrams: Adjectives and Adverbs.

items: Direct object: after the verb, behind a short upright line that stops at the baseline (only the subject–verb line crosses it).
Indirect object: on a flat line hung under the verb by a slant.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: Grandma gave Sam a new book.

blocks.cap: Gave what? book (on the baseline). To whom? Sam (under the verb).

blocks.html: Two upright lines on the baseline mean two different things: the one that crosses splits subject from verb; the one that stops at the line comes before the direct object.
The line types encode the jobs. Anyone who knows the code can read a diagram and see which noun receives the action and which one is the receiver of the thing given.

blocks.title: Two objects
blocks.q: Diagram “The coach handed the team a map.”
steps: Baseline: coach | handed | map (handed what?).
The under coach; a under map.
To whom? team: on a flat line under handed, with the hanging from it.
blocks.a: coach | handed | map, with team under handed

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: Leo baked his sister a cake.

blocks.cap: Build it, then Check.

blocks.html: Drawing the line before a direct object all the way through the baseline. That crossing line is the mark of the subject–verb split. The object line stops at the baseline.

sources.name: Alonzo Reed and Brainerd Kellogg, Higher Lessons in English (1877; revised edition 1896), Project Gutenberg eBook #7188 (public domain): the diagrams of Lessons 4–33
Grokipedia, “Sentence diagram”

blocks.html: Complements that rename or describe something get a slanted line instead of an upright one. The slant leans back toward the word they point to. This builds on Diagrams: Direct and Indirect Objects and Object Complements.

items: A predicate noun or predicate adjective follows the verb, behind a line slanted back toward the subject.
An object complement follows the direct object, behind a line slanted back toward the object.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: My sister became the captain.

blocks.cap: Captain renames the subject, so its line slants back toward it.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: They named the puppy Biscuit.

blocks.cap: Biscuit renames the object, so its line slants back toward puppy.

blocks.html: Upright line: the word receives the action (direct object). Slanted line: the word renames or describes the subject or the object.
The slant is a little arrow pointing back. It shows that the captain is the sister and that Biscuit is the puppy, which is exactly what makes them complements and not objects.

blocks.title: A predicate adjective
blocks.q: Diagram “The soup smelled delicious.”
steps: Baseline: soup | smelled.
Smelled is linking here; delicious describes the soup.
Write delicious after a line slanted back toward soup. The hangs under soup.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: The news made Dad happy.

blocks.cap: Build it. Which word gets the slanted line?

blocks.html: Using the direct-object line for a predicate noun. In “Mia became captain,” nothing receives an action; the slant points back to the word the complement renames or describes.
Reed and Kellogg called the predicate noun or adjective an “attribute complement” and drew the same slanted line before it.

Grokipedia, “Subject complement”
Grokipedia, “Object complement”

blocks.html: A prepositional phrase is a modifier, so it hangs under the word it modifies (Diagrams: Adjectives and Adverbs). It gets two lines: the preposition on a slanted line, and its object on a flat line at the bottom of the slant. The object’s own modifiers hang under it.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: The girl with the kite ran to the park.

blocks.cap: An adjective phrase under girl; an adverb phrase under ran.

blocks.html: Hang each phrase under the word it tells about. That is not always the nearest word.
The diagram forces the question every reader asks silently: what does this phrase go with? Answering it is how you spot and fix unclear sentences.

blocks.title: Not the nearest word
blocks.q: Diagram “Leo kicked the ball over the fence.”
steps: Baseline: Leo | kicked | ball.
over the fence tells where he kicked, so it hangs under kicked, not under ball.
over on the slant, fence on the flat line, the under fence.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: Leo kicked the ball over the fence.

blocks.cap: Step through the diagram word by word.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: The cat on the porch slept in the sun.

blocks.cap: Build it, then Check.

blocks.html: Hanging the phrase under the nearest word instead of the word it modifies. Ask: does it tell which one (hang it from the noun) or where, when, how (hang it from the verb)?

blocks.html: Compound parts (Compound Subjects and Verbs) split the line into a fork: parallel lines, one for each part, joined by a dashed line with the conjunction beside it. This builds on objects and phrases.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: Ana and Leo sang and danced.

blocks.cap: A compound subject and a compound verb on one baseline.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: Dad washed and dried the dishes.

blocks.cap: Both verbs share one direct object, so the fork closes again before it.

blocks.html: A compound sentence has two independent clauses, so it gets two baselines, one above the other. A dashed line, shaped like a step, joins the two verbs, with the conjunction on it.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: The rain stopped, and the sun came out.

blocks.cap: Two clauses, two baselines.

blocks.html: Compound parts of one clause: a fork on one baseline. Two independent clauses: two baselines. The conjunction never sits on the baseline; it goes beside the dashed line.

The fork shows that the parts share a job (two subjects for one verb, two verbs for one subject). Two baselines show two complete clauses. The difference is the difference between a simple sentence with compound parts and a compound sentence.

blocks.title: Fork or two baselines?
blocks.q: “Leo sang and danced” and “Leo sang, and Mia danced.”
steps: First: one subject, two verbs: a fork for the verbs on one baseline.
Second: two subjects, each with its own verb: two baselines joined by and.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: Mia bought apples and pears.

blocks.cap: Build the compound direct object, then Check.

blocks.html: Putting the conjunction on the baseline, or drawing one baseline for a compound sentence. A compound sentence has two subjects with two verbs; give each clause its own baseline.

Grokipedia, “Sentence diagram”

blocks.html: An appositive renames the noun beside it, so in a diagram it sits beside that noun, in parentheses, on the same line. Its own modifiers hang under it. This builds on Diagrams: Complements.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: My aunt, a pilot, flew the plane.

blocks.cap: (pilot) stands beside aunt; a hangs under it.

blocks.html: Some words are not part of the sentence’s frame at all: interjections (wow, oh) and nouns of direct address (the name of the person spoken to). Each sits on its own short line above the baseline.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: Wow, close the door quickly!

blocks.cap: The interjection floats above. The subject of the command is (you).

blocks.html: Renames the noun? Beside it, in parentheses. Not part of the sentence’s frame (interjection, direct address)? On a line above.

An appositive is the same thing as its noun, so it shares the noun’s place on the line. Interjections and names in direct address do no job inside the sentence, so they sit apart, just as commas set them apart in writing.

blocks.title: A name in direct address
blocks.q: Diagram “Leo, close the window.”
steps: A command: the subject is (you).
Baseline: (you) | close | window, with the under window.
Leo is the person spoken to: on a short line above the baseline.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: Mr. Lee, our coach, blew the whistle.

blocks.cap: Build it, then Check.

blocks.html: Hanging an appositive under the noun as if it were an adjective. An appositive doesn’t describe the noun; it renames it, so it stands beside it.
Reed and Kellogg called an appositive an “explanatory modifier” and wrote it “enclosed in curves” (parentheses), as here.

blocks.html: Verbals (participles, gerunds and infinitives) are verb forms doing other jobs, so they never go on the baseline as the main verb. Each has its own line shape. This builds on prepositional phrases and complements.

head: Verbal
Its job
Its line
rows: a slant that bends into a flat line, under the noun it modifies
a stepped line, raised on a forked stand in a noun’s place
to on a slant and the verb on a flat line; on a forked stand when it does a noun’s job

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: Swimming in the lake cools the tired hikers.

blocks.cap: A gerund phrase as the subject (on its stand) and a participle under hikers.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: Leo wants to win.

blocks.cap: An infinitive as the direct object, on a stand in the object’s place.

blocks.html: Find the real verb first and put it on the baseline. Then give each verbal the line of its job: bent (participle), stepped (gerund), or to on a slant (infinitive).

The shapes show that these words are still verbs inside (they can have objects and modifiers) but do a noun’s or an adjective’s job outside. The forked stand lifts a whole verbal phrase into a single noun place.

blocks.title: A participial phrase
blocks.q: Diagram “Waving her hat, Mia ran.”
steps: The real verb is ran; the subject is Mia.
Waving her hat describes Mia, so it hangs under Mia on a bent line.
hat is the object of waving; her hangs under hat.
blocks.a: Mia | ran, with waving | hat under Mia

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: Waving her hat, Mia ran.

blocks.cap: Step through it.

blocks.html: Putting a verbal on the baseline as if it were the main verb. In “Swimming cools the hikers,” the verb is cools; swimming is the subject, so it stands on a stand in the subject’s place.

Grokipedia, “Sentence diagram”

blocks.html: A complex sentence has a dependent clause, and a clause has its own subject and verb, so it gets its own baseline below the main one. A dotted line joins it to the word it modifies. This builds on Diagrams: Compound Parts and Sentences.

items: Adverb clause: the dotted line runs from the verb (or other word) it modifies down to the clause’s verb. The subordinating conjunction sits on the dotted line.
Adjective clause: the dotted line runs from the noun it modifies down to the relative pronoun, which sits in its own job inside the clause (subject, object …).

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: We left when the bell rang.

blocks.cap: An adverb clause: when on the dotted line from left to rang.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: The book that you lent me is great.

blocks.cap: An adjective clause: the dotted line runs from book to that, the direct object of lent.

blocks.html: Each clause gets its own baseline. Adverb clause: conjunction on the dotted line. Adjective clause: the relative pronoun stays inside its clause, and the dotted line reaches it.

The two baselines show the two clauses; the dotted line shows which word the dependent clause depends on. That answers the question that causes most misplaced clauses: what does this clause tell about?

blocks.title: The relative pronoun’s job
blocks.q: In “The girl who won the race is my cousin,” where does who go?
steps: The clause is who won the race.
Inside it, who is the subject of won.
So who goes in the subject place of the clause’s baseline, and the dotted line runs from girl to who.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: Mia smiled when she saw the puppy.

blocks.cap: Build it, then Check.

blocks.html: Attaching the clause to the wrong word, or leaving the relative pronoun off the clause’s baseline when it is the clause’s subject or object. Ask what the relative pronoun does inside its own clause.

blocks.html: A noun clause is a noun, not a modifier, so it doesn’t hang from anything. Like a gerund (Diagrams: Participles, Gerunds and Infinitives), it stands on a forked stand in the place a noun would go: subject, direct object, predicate noun or object of a preposition. It keeps its own baseline on top of the stand. This builds on Diagrams: Adjective and Adverb Clauses.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: I know that she left.

blocks.cap: The noun clause is the direct object. That only introduces it, so it sits on a short line above, joined by a dotted line.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: What you said surprised me.

blocks.cap: The noun clause is the subject. Inside it, What is the direct object of said.

blocks.html: A noun clause stands on a stand in a noun’s place. A word like that or whether, which only introduces the clause, sits on a line above it; a word like what or who, which does a job inside the clause, goes in that job’s place.

The stand shows the clause doing a noun’s job in the main sentence while keeping its own subject and verb. It is the same idea as a gerund on its stand: something bigger than a word, used as one noun.

blocks.title: A noun clause as predicate noun
blocks.q: Diagram “My hope is that the rain stops.”
steps: Main baseline: hope | is, with My under hope.
The clause renames hope: it is the predicate noun, after the slanted line.
It stands on a stand there: rain | stops, the under rain, and that above.

opts.text: My hope is that the rain stops.

blocks.name: wr-diagram

opts.text: We know that the bus is late.

blocks.cap: Build it, then Check.

blocks.html: Attaching a noun clause with a dotted line as if it were a modifier. Use the “something” test: “I know something.” The clause is the object itself, so it stands in the object’s place.

Textbooks draw a few details differently (the angle of a slant, where a conjunction sits). These lessons use the usual form, as in Reed and Kellogg’s Higher Lessons in English and most American grammars; if your book differs a little, both are fine.
